newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lufthansa sell-off could start in 96.
newsitem.headline: Lufthansa sell-off could start in 96.

text.p: The final stage of Deutsche Lufthansa AG's privatisation could now start this year after Bonn on Friday said it was ready to sell its remaining 35.7 percent stake in the German airline to a trustee.

The announcement followed Thursday's pact between the German government and the European Commission on measures to ensure the carrier does not fall into foreign control after the sale, which would violate international air traffic rules.

The government said it was now considering passing on the Lufthansa stake to an intermediary before the end of 1996, for a sale to the market in the second half in 1997 which would generate some 2.9 billion marks ($2 billion) for its cash-starved coffers.

Fears over the risk of loss of German control over the airline and the prospect of next week's mega-flotation of Deutsche Telekom stock had been expected to delay the start of the Lufthansa sell-off process until next year.

But Adolf Roth, a budget expert from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democratic party (CDU), said the interim measure would allow Bonn to count at least part of the Lufthansa revenue towards reducing its public debt.
Separately, the Finance Ministry said it was already in talks to set up a similar system to sell off its six percent stake in DG Bank understood to be worth around 500 million marks.

News of the impending stake transfer had a calming effect on Lufthansa's stock, which ended bourse trade unchanged at 20.25 marks, after coming under pressure Thursday on fears the EU pact would put foreign investors at a disadvantage.
"The privatisation issue has been hovering around Lufthansa shares for a long time and now it looks like this will end," said Martin Wirth, analyst at Bank Julius Baer, Frankfurt.

Wirth said the news was broadly positive, but added: "In the final analysis, it's irrelevant who Lufthansa's main shareholder is. Lufthansa is not like Air France -- it gets no special treatment or subsidies from Bonn."
The government on Friday would not reveal which intermediary would take on the Lufthansa package.
Handelsblatt, Germany's leading economic daily, reported that the most likely taker was the Frankfurt-based state-owned development bank Kreditanstalt fuer Wiederaufbau (KfW).
The Finance Ministry confirmed that KfW was among the banks involved in talks, it said this was not the only option.
KfW, which already owns around three percent of Lufthansa, said there had been no final decision on the deal.

The German government has retained its minority stake in Lufthansa since the carrier was partially privatised in 1994, but has been keen to sell the holding to reduce its public debt. Procceds from privatisation cannot be used under European Union rules to reduce running budget deficits - a key element in measuring a country's eligibility for monetary union.

On Thursday, Germany's transport ministry agreed with the EU to set up a transition period during the sale of the Lufthansa stake, giving Bonn limited rights to buy back shares if the German majority in the airline is threatened.
International air law requires that flag carriers demonstrate their nation's shareholders hold majority stakes in order to meet the conditions of around 200 bilateral air agreements.
Lufthansa's stock, weighed on by weak earnings reports, have lost more than a fifth of their value this year since hitting a high of 25.98 marks last April.

Lufthansa chief executive Juergen Weber said in a German newspaper interview this week that the airline expects to earn about as much in 1996 as it did in 1995, but warned that return on sales would not be satisfactory.
The Frankfurt-based airline in 1995 reported a group profit from ordinary activities of 756.3 million marks while the return on sales was 3.8 percent. ($1=1.5063 Mark)
